resources.string: This action performs “%1$s”. Automatic mode selects an available supported backend at runtime; it does not itself grant Root, Shizuku, or any other access.
This trigger observes “%1$s”. Automatic mode selects an available supported event path; the selected path still needs its own access.
This condition checks “%1$s”. Automatic mode uses an available check path; the data it can inspect depends on that backend's permissions.
This state reads “%1$s”. Automatic mode selects an available state-reading path; it cannot bypass Android access controls by itself.
To perform “%1$s”, the Root backend executes the privileged steps through su. YAuto must be authorized by the Root manager.
To observe “%1$s”, the Root backend uses privileged access to event sources that ordinary apps may not read. su access is required.
To check “%1$s”, the Root backend reads restricted system information via su; ordinary app permissions alone may not suffice.
To read “%1$s”, the Root backend accesses the relevant privileged system state. Root-manager authorization is required.
To perform “%1$s”, the Shizuku backend runs the relevant system command with the service's shell identity, not unrestricted Root access.
To observe “%1$s”, the Shizuku backend uses shell-level access to the required event source; its service must remain running.
To check “%1$s”, the Shizuku backend queries the required system information as shell; shell restrictions still apply.
To read “%1$s”, the Shizuku backend queries the corresponding system state as shell; available data depends on Android shell privileges.
To perform “%1$s”, the LSPosed backend uses Hooks in the scoped target process for the relevant system or app call; the correct scope is essential.
To observe “%1$s”, the LSPosed backend hooks events in the selected target process; enable the module and the appropriate scope.
To check “%1$s”, the LSPosed backend uses Hooks to inspect the corresponding internal state; scope and OS version matter.
To read “%1$s”, the LSPosed backend obtains state accessible through scoped process Hooks, not unrestricted access to all app data.
To perform “%1$s”, the Accessibility backend uses accessible UI nodes or Android accessibility actions; the YAuto service must be enabled.
To observe “%1$s”, the Accessibility backend listens for UI events exposed to the service; unavailable events cannot be detected.
To check “%1$s”, the Accessibility backend inspects accessible UI state; controls hidden from the service may not be detectable.
To read “%1$s”, the Accessibility backend uses information accessible to the service in the current UI, not privileged system reads.
For “%1$s”, Usage Access provides app-usage or foreground-activity records only; it cannot itself perform protected system actions.
To observe “%1$s”, Usage Access relies on Android usage records rather than real-time Accessibility events.
To check “%1$s”, Usage Access queries Android's app-usage records; recording latency can affect results.
To read “%1$s”, Usage Access queries permitted Android usage state, not private internal state of every app.
Note: Root access is highly privileged; results still depend on the device, Android version, and command involved.
Note: shell is more restricted than Root, so some operations may fail; Shizuku may need restarting after reboot.
Note: Hook scope and Android/ROM versions affect results; changing Hooks can require restarting the target process.
Note: UI accessibility can be limited with the screen off, hidden controls, or custom-rendered app interfaces.
Note: usage records may lag and do not expose complete screen content or privileged control.
